newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Russia overseas debt, shares rise on Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia overseas debt, shares rise on Yeltsin.

text.p: Russian debt and equity traded overseas reacted positively to news that President Boris Yeltsin's heart operation has been completed and the market is now expected to test new highs.
Vneshekonombank debt was up two points on Tuesday before news of the completion of the operation and added a further half point to reach 78 3/8 percent of face value after it was over.
"The deal risk in Russia is disappearing and the market could trade to the mid-80s over the next few weeks," said a Russian debt trader at a U.S. bank in London.
At its peak of 80 percent of face value early last month, Russian debt had risen 150 percent from the start of this year, making it the best performing asset in its class.
Russia will start the roadshow for its $300-$500 million eurbond issue in London next week and this will give a further fillip to prices, traders said.
"What we are looking for now is evidence that Yeltsin is making a full recovery and easing back in to the seat of power," said the trader.

If Yeltsin does recover fully, then he will keep the factions in his government in check and pursue further reforms. But if the president is incapacitated then his fractious cabinet could see further infighting.
"Reform in Russia needs a strong hand. Someone needs to convince the International Monetary Fund to keep on handing over the cash, and the only person who can do that is Yeltsin," said the trader.
The IMF quit Moscow last month without opening its coffers to disburse further funds from its $10.2 billion loan for Russia as it warned that tax collection was not strong enough.
Among Russian equities traded overseas, American Depositary Shares in gas giant Gazprom were firm, rising from up two cents before the operation to up 10 cents at $17.50/$18.00 after its completion.

Gazprom completed the largest international share offering from a Russian company last month when it raised a total of $430 million from foreign investors in an issue that was five times oversubscribed. "Russian equities are a play for the medium and longer-term," said Matt Linsey, an emerging markets fund manager for ING in Luxembourg.
He favours access to the market through stocks which have not yet seen large flows of foreign money, such as electricity utility Irkutskenergo.
"What we are looking for is lots of productive capacity that is worth something, not a company that requires vast amounts of capital expenditure," Linsey said.
Others cautioned that some profit taking could erode some of the immediate gains made by the debt and equity markets.
"We are already seeing dealers locking in some of the debt market's gains after the operation but longer term, buyers will emerge," said the debt trader at the U.S. bank.
Share traders believe that companies such as Gazprom and department store GUM, which is over 40 percent owned by foreign investors, could see some of their gains pegged back.

"If I were looking for Russian exposure, I would be selling my Gazprom ADS and buying in the local market. A lot of these shares have had a huge run and the way to make real money is to go for second-line shares," said a trader at a leading European bank in London.
